transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-08-25
Start: 16:30 PT
Duration: ~56 minutes
Attendees: Avery Kim (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Dr. Priya Nair (CTO, Coppergate), Mark Jensen (Infra Lead), Sofia Alvarez (Compliance)

Summary (auto): Intake call to surface Coppergate's on-prem legacy hardware constraints, offline update/courier requirements, and compliance expectations. Discussed possible private/on-prem deployment models, signed-package offline update patterns, and PoC next steps.

[00:00] Avery (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you making time. Quick intros — I'm Avery on the account side, Diego is our solutions engineer, and we'll mostly listen then dig into technical questions. 
[00:18] Priya (Coppergate CTO): Hi — Priya here, thanks. We've got Mark from infra and Sofia from compliance. We're trying to figure out if Redwood can run on our old datacenter stuff and how updates would work with zero internet.
[00:27] Diego (Redwood SE): Great, quick clarifying question — when you say "old datacenter stuff," can you give us the GPU types and the OS baseline? Even approximate helps.
[00:36] Mark: Yeah, so our fleet is kind of mixed. Majority are Dell R740s with NVIDIA Tesla P100 cards, a handful of older T4s, and a couple lab servers with non-NVIDIA accelerators we use for batch workloads. OS is RHEL 7 for most nodes; a few CentOS 7.3 still hanging around.
[00:54] Avery: Okay that's helpful — and the network situation? Fully air-gapped, no egress at all?
[01:02] Priya: Correct, no outbound to the internet. We have a strict change window policy and any external media must go via an approved courier with chain-of-custody.
[01:10] Sofia: And from compliance perspective, any update has to be signed and verifiable. We use internal HSM for signing, we can't allow unsigned binaries in. SOC2 and a few other attestation points are required.
[01:22] Diego: Understood. So two main constraints: hardware compatibility with older cards and an offline, signed-package update process with physical transfer. Both are things we've done before but the details matter — firmware versions, kernel modules, CUDA compatibility.
[01:36] Mark: Right — for example we can't move kernels easily; our ops team avoids kernel upgrades unless absolutely necessary. That limits us from using certain newer runtimes that expect modern glibc or CUDA stacks.
[01:46] (crosstalk)
[01:48] Avery: Diego, can you explain at a high level what Redwood Private would look like in this environment? Like an architecture sketch?
[01:56] Diego: Sure. On-prem Private deploy runs a control plane that can be either fully customer-hosted or a hybrid where the control plane is in the customer VPC — but in your case with zero egress we'll push for a fully self-contained control plane. The serving runtime runs as containers on each node and we provide a signed bundle for offline install. The CLI and agent can be installed from the bundle and validated against your HSM-signed manifest.
[02:20] Priya: When you say signed bundle, who signs? We need to use our HSM — we can't accept Redwood's signatures unless they are co-signed.
[02:28] Diego: That's doable. We support a co-signing pattern: Redwood produces the package and a digest; you verify and sign with your H M S; the install flow validates both signatures. We have shipped an example flow where the installer checks both Redwood's artifact signature and the customer's on-device KMS signature.
[02:43] Mark: Any idea about how big those bundles are? We have strict limits on what can be transferred by courier in a single package — also parity with incremental patches would be ideal.
[02:52] Diego: Base bundle could be several gigabytes, depending on model weights you include. For incremental patches we build delta packages — smaller, signed diffs — so you don't have to transport full model weights every time. Very common in air-gapped customers.
[03:06] Sofia: What about KMS access during runtime? We can't have a cloud KMS reachback.
[03:11] Diego: Right — for Private air-gapped deployments we support local KMS/HSM integrations. The runtime can call a local HSM over PKCS#11 or via an isolated appliance. No outbound network calls required.
[03:21] Priya: Okay good. Does Redwood require anything like a heartbeat to your hosted services for license checks?
[03:27] Avery: Short answer, no. For private/offline we can do license files and local license servers that operate without internet. We prefer automatic telemetry for ops but it's optional and can be disabled for compliance.
[03:40] Mark: Performance question — with P100s, are we likely to hit our throughput goals? We need about 50 tokens/sec per GPU for our internal routing tasks.
[03:49] Diego: P100 is older but still viable. Throughput per card depends on model size and whether you use quantized variants. With optimized kernels and lower precision paths we can approach that ballpark for medium-sized models (7B-ish). We'll need to run a small benchmark PoC to be certain.
[04:05] Priya: We do have a hard requirement that any PoC run has to not push secrets externally and not leave logs offsite. 
[04:12] Diego: Absolutely. For PoC we supply a self-contained benchmark harness that runs locally, stores logs locally, and produces a signed report you can review. We can also ship a pre-built container so no network is required.
[04:24] Avery: Let's talk about update cadence — how are customers typically doing monthly security patches in a zero- internet environment?
[04:31] Mark: Right now it's messy — we get vendor ISOs on USB, they go through security scanning, and then someone physically installs them during a maintenance window. Takes days of coordination.
[04:39] Diego: Our pattern: Redwood builds release artifacts and publishes a signed digest. For air-gapped sites we produce an offline bundle and a delta. The bundle includes an installer that validates signatures against the co-signed manifest. The customer copies the bundle into the air-gapped network through their courier process. Installer runs during your maintenance window and reports a local install log.
[04:57] Sofia: The chain-of-custody is important — we need tamper-evident packaging and a recorded handoff.
[05:03] Avery: We don't handle courier ourselves, typically the customer uses their approved logistic partner. But we can provide checksums, signed manifests, and step-by-step install verification documentation for chain-of-custody records.
[05:15] Priya: Two compliance concerns — first: provenance of model weights. We need to show where model weights came from and any training data lineage. Second: attestation for runtime integrity.
[05:27] Diego: For provenance we include model metadata with hashes and a provenance file. For runtime attestation we can support signed boot and measured boot patterns as part of the image; additionally, we provide a runtime integrity check that records a signed report that can be stored locally for audits.
[05:44] Mark: Are you able to support older CUDA versions? Our fleet is on CUDA 9.2 for some nodes, and upgrading would require coordination with vendor drivers.
[05:53] Diego: CUDA 9.2 is challenging; a lot of newer kernels and attention optimizations target CUDA 11+. We can build legacy runtime images that support older CUDA stacks but there are limits — some operator perf features and quantized kernels won't be available. That's a tradeoff: maintainability and performance vs non-invasive upgrades.
[06:12] Priya: If we opt for legacy runtimes, what's the upgrade path later?
[06:16] Diego: We recommend a staged approach. Start with legacy runtime to get you into production, run PoC and gather metrics, then plan an upgrade path for a subset of nodes to modern runtime over 3-6 months. The Control Plane supports routing traffic to mixed runtime pools, so you can do canary transitions.
[06:30] (overlap)
[06:31] Sofia: On the legal side, we need indemnity language around data exfiltration vectors and also evidence of secure coding and S-S-S-S? sorry, SAST results.
[06:41] Avery: We can share our security whitepaper, SAST/SCA summaries, and SOC2 Type II report. For indemnity we can bring legal into the conversation once we have a baseline SLA and deployment form.
[06:52] Diego: A few operational notes — we advise customers to provide a hardware manifest that lists CPU, GPU, driver versions, BIOS firmware versions. Even patch-level differences in vendor firmware can cause mismatches with accelerated kernels.
[07:06] Mark: We'll pull that together. Another question: what about offline telemetry? We sometimes want to collect and ship back logs for support but that's a separate courier flow.
[07:15] Diego: Yes, we support optional offline log collection. Support bundles can be generated locally with a single command and then transferred out via your courier. We can provide guidelines for what to include to minimize export of PII.
[07:25] Priya: What about cost — how does pricing change with Private/dedicated vs hosted? We want rough numbers to justify procurement.
[07:33] Avery: Hosted is pay-as-you-go and lower upfront. Private has a platform license plus per-node fees; dedicated (reserved) is in between with monthly commits. For an air-gapped private deployment there's typically a one-time onboarding fee for offline artifacts and custom packaging. We'll follow up with a tailored pricing sheet once we have node counts.
[07:49] Priya: Timeline — procurement wants a vendor recommendation by end of Q3. We're in late August now, so that's tight.
[07:56] Avery: We can accelerate: security docs and initial PoC scope out this week, PoC run two weeks after you hand over hardware manifest. If all goes well, a recommendation by late September is doable.
[08:07] Mark: For the PoC we'd prefer a minimal footprint: two nodes, local model only, 24-hour soak, and performance report.
[08:15] Diego: That's a standard PoC. We'll define token/sec targets and latency SLOs in the scope doc.
[08:21] Sofia: On attestations again, do you provide signed SBOMs for runtime images?
[08:26] Diego: Yes we can generate SBOMs and sign them. We also produce a manifest with component hashes for your audit team.
[08:34] Priya: One more operational nuance — our facility restricts USB vendors. We might need to do a direct SFTP from a staging net to a sealed network via an insulated transfer appliance. Does Redwood support a staged import that verifies integrity post-transfer?
[08:48] Diego: Yes, the installer has a verification phase that checks signatures and digests before extracting. We also support importing via an internal staging server where you upload signed bundles and the installer pulls from that local endpoint.
[08:59] (brief pause)
[09:02] Priya: Are there known customers who run on P100 fleets or similar that you can point to?
[09:08] Avery: We have references in regulated verticals who started on older GPUs and transitioned; we'll share anonymized case studies.
[09:14] Mark: On the topic of model weights provenance — would you allow us to freeze a particular model version and then prevent automatic updates?
[09:22] Diego: Absolutely. You can pin model versions and control rollout; we won't auto-update weights in a Private deployment unless you opt-in. That helps with validation and compliance.
[09:33] Sofia: Does Redwood offer any on-site support? We have restricted vendor access but sometimes we need an engineer on-site to assist with install during the first rollout.
[09:41] Avery: Yes, we offer professional services engagements for initial onboarding, and we've done on-site installs where customers require it. Those are scheduled and use background-checked staff.
[09:50] Diego: From the SE side, we can also remote in via your bastion during the maintenance window — obviously only if you allow and we follow your access policies.
[09:59] Priya: Ok — let's talk network segmentation briefly. We use strict VLAN separation; can Redwood agent be constrained to a single VLAN and not need any cross-vlan routing?
[10:08] Diego: Yes — the runtime components are containerized and can bind to the interfaces you allow. No requirement to cross to management VLANs if you route properly.
[10:16] Mark: For auditability, we want logs in append-only storage and hashed daily snapshots. Is that supported?
[10:21] Diego: You can configure local log retention to a mounted append-only volume. Our agent can produce daily hashed snapshots which you can ingest into your audit system.
[10:31] (short silence)
[10:33] Avery: Ok, near the end here — let's recap and set concrete next steps. Diego, do you want to summarise the technical actions?
[10:40] Diego: Sure — I'll prepare a PoC scope for a 2-node run, benchmark harness, and a list of runtime images (legacy + modern) we'll provide. I'll also sketch the signed-package flow for your H M S co-signing. Expect that by 2026-09-08.
[10:55] Avery: I'll share security docs and SOC2 writeup by 2026-09-01 and an anonymized case study. 
[11:02] Mark: I'll upload the hardware manifest, firmware inventory and preferred patch windows by 2026-09-03.
[11:08] Sofia: I'll confirm compliance stakeholders and required attestations by 2026-09-05.
[11:12] Priya: Sounds good. Couple of open items — we need a rough cost estimate to put in procurement — please include estimated one-time onboarding fee and a ballpark per-node price.
[11:20] Avery: Absolutely, we'll include a high-level cost sheet in the follow-up.
[11:25] (end recap)

Closing notes: conversation had realistic friction points — legacy CUDA/CUDF constraints, offline signed-package flow, chain-of-custody, H M S co-signing and SBOMs. No unresolved red flags; next steps and owners assigned.
